mil5.2.5:0.4: 5.  Question on Obstruction to the Buddha’s Gains
mil5.2.5:1.2: ‘The Tathāgata is a receiver of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick.’
mil5.2.5:1.3: And yet the Tathāgata, having entered the brahmin village of Pañcasālā for alms, got nothing at all and left with his bowl as clean as if it had been washed.
mil5.2.5:1.4: If, Venerable Nāgasena, the Tathāgata is a receiver of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites, then the statement that he entered Pañcasālā for alms, got nothing, and left with his bowl just as if it had been washed is false.
mil5.2.5:1.5: If, Venerable Nāgasena, the Tathāgata is a receiver of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites, then the statement that he entered Pañcasālā for alms, got nothing, and left with his bowl just as if it had been washed is also false.
mil5.2.5:1.6: This too is a double-horned question, very great and hard to untie, that has come to you; you must resolve it.”
mil5.2.5:2.1: “Your majesty, the Tathāgata is a receiver of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites, and he did enter Pañcasālā for alms, get nothing, and leave with his bowl as if it had been washed. But that was because of Māra the Evil One.”
mil5.2.5:2.2: “Then, Venerable Nāgasena, how was the wholesome kamma the Blessed One accumulated over aeons beyond counting brought to an end? How was the force and power of that wholesome kamma blocked by Māra the Evil One, who had only just arisen?
mil5.2.5:2.3: In that case, Venerable Nāgasena, blame attaches to this episode in two respects: the unwholesome would be stronger than the wholesome, and Māra’s power stronger than the Buddha’s power.
mil5.2.5:2.4: That would be like saying the tip of a tree is heavier than its root, or that evil is stronger than one who is filled with virtues.”
mil5.2.5:2.5: In that case, Venerable Nāgasena, blame attaches to this episode in two respects: the unwholesome would be stronger than the wholesome, and Māra’s power stronger than the Buddha’s power.
mil5.2.5:2.6: But a reason is desirable here.
mil5.2.5:3.1: Suppose, your majesty, a man brought honey, or a honey-cake, or some other gift to a wheel-turning monarch, and the king’s doorkeeper said to him: ‘It is the wrong time, sir, to see the king. So take your gift and go back quickly, or else your king will impose a penalty on you.’
mil5.2.5:3.2: Then that man, trembling and anxious from fear of punishment, would take his gift and hurry back. Would that wheel-turning monarch, your majesty, become weaker than the doorkeeper merely because of that much, the lack of that gift? Or would he be unable to receive any other gift?”
mil5.2.5:3.3: “Certainly not, venerable sir. That doorkeeper, out of jealousy, turned the gift away; but through another door the king receives gifts a hundred thousand times greater.”
mil5.2.5:3.4: “In just the same way, your majesty, Māra the Evil One, driven by jealousy, took possession of the brahmin householders of Pañcasālā; but many hundreds of thousands of other deities, bringing divine, immortal nutriment, stood there with palms joined and paying homage to the Blessed One, thinking, ‘We will place nutriment in the Blessed One’s body.’”
mil5.2.5:4.1: “Granted, Venerable Nāgasena, that the four requisites are easily obtained in the world by the Blessed One, the supreme person, and that the Blessed One uses the four requisites only when asked by devas and humans. Still, Māra’s purpose was accomplished to that extent, in that he created an obstruction to the Blessed One’s meal.
mil5.2.5:4.2: On this point, venerable sir, my doubt is not cut off; I am perplexed and caught in uncertainty.
mil5.2.5:4.3: My mind does not settle on this: that Māra, a base, low, trifling, evil, ignoble, ruined being, could create an obstruction to the gains of the Tathāgata, the arahant, the perfectly Awakened One, the foremost individual in the world with its devas, born of the finest wholesome merit, without equal, incomparable, unmatched.”
mil5.2.5:5.1: “Your majesty, there are four kinds of obstruction: an obstruction to what is unseen; an obstruction made with a particular person in mind; an obstruction to what has been prepared; and an obstruction to use.
mil5.2.5:5.2: Then which is the obstruction to what is unseen?
mil5.2.5:5.3: When someone, without having a particular person in mind and without seeing anyone, obstructs something not yet prepared, thinking ‘What is the use of giving to others?’ This is called the obstruction to what is unseen.
mil5.2.5:6.1: Which is the obstruction made with a particular person in mind?
mil5.2.5:6.2: When food has been prepared with a certain person indicated and in mind, and someone obstructs it. This is called the obstruction made with a particular person in mind.
mil5.2.5:7.1: Which is the obstruction to what has been prepared?
mil5.2.5:7.2: When something has been prepared but not yet accepted, and someone obstructs it. This is called the obstruction to what has been prepared.
mil5.2.5:8.1: Which is the obstruction to use?
mil5.2.5:8.2: When something is available for use, and someone obstructs it. This is called the obstruction to use.
mil5.2.5:8.3: These, your majesty, are the four obstructions.
mil5.2.5:9.1: Now what Māra the Evil One did when he took possession of the brahmin householders of Pañcasālā was not an obstruction to the Blessed One’s use, nor to something prepared, nor to something made with him in mind. It was an obstruction made in his absence, for something not yet come and not yet arrived. Moreover it was not only for the Blessed One; all those who went out at that time and arrived there also failed to get food that day. I do not see, your majesty, anyone in the world with its devas, Māras and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics, brahmins, devas and humans, who could obstruct the use of what has been prepared and made ready with the Blessed One in mind.
mil5.2.5:9.2: If anyone out of jealousy were to obstruct what has been prepared and made ready with him in mind, his head would split into a hundred or a thousand pieces.
mil5.2.5:10.1: There are, your majesty, four qualities of the Tathāgata that cannot be obstructed by anyone.
mil5.2.5:10.3: The gain prepared and made ready with the Blessed One in mind cannot be obstructed by anyone.
mil5.2.5:10.4: The fathom-wide radiance that accompanies the Blessed One’s body cannot be obstructed by anyone.
mil5.2.5:10.5: The Blessed One’s jewel of knowledge, his omniscience, cannot be obstructed by anyone.
mil5.2.5:10.6: The Blessed One’s life cannot be obstructed by anyone.
mil5.2.5:10.7: These, your majesty, are the four qualities of the Tathāgata that cannot be obstructed by anyone. All these qualities, your majesty, are of one flavour: free of disease, unshakable, beyond the reach of any attack, untouchable by action.
mil5.2.5:10.8: It was by remaining unseen, your majesty, that Māra the Evil One hid himself and took possession of the brahmin householders of Pañcasālā.
mil5.2.5:11.1: Just as, your majesty, in a rough border region of a king’s realm, robbers hide unseen and spoil the road.
mil5.2.5:11.2: But if the king were to see those robbers, would they find safety?”
mil5.2.5:11.3: “Certainly not, venerable sir. He would have them split with an axe into a hundred or a thousand pieces.”
mil5.2.5:11.4: “In just the same way, your majesty, Māra the Evil One hid unseen and took possession of the brahmin householders of Pañcasālā.
mil5.2.5:12.1: Or again, your majesty, it is like a married woman who hides unseen and consorts with another man.
mil5.2.5:12.2: In just the same way, Māra the Evil One hid unseen and took possession of the brahmin householders of Pañcasālā.
mil5.2.5:12.3: If, your majesty, that woman were to consort with another man in front of her husband, would she find safety?”
mil5.2.5:12.4: “Certainly not, Venerable Sir. The husband might kill her, or beat her, or bind her, or reduce her to slavery.”
mil5.2.5:12.5: “In just the same way, your majesty, Māra the Evil One hid unseen and took possession of the brahmin householders of Pañcasālā.
mil5.2.5:12.6: If Māra the Evil One had obstructed what had been prepared and made ready with the Blessed One in mind, his head would split into a hundred or a thousand pieces.”
mil5.2.5:12.7: “So it is, Venerable Nāgasena, Māra the Evil One acted like a thief, hiding unseen and taking possession of the brahmin householders of Pañcasālā.
mil5.2.5:12.8: Had that Māra obstructed the use of what was prepared and made ready with the Blessed One in mind, his head would have split into a hundred or a thousand pieces, or his body would have scattered like a handful of chaff.
mil5.2.5:12.9: Well said, Venerable Nāgasena; I accept it so.”
